Torment
TOR-ment
n., v.
From Latin tormentum, an instrument of torture, from torquere, to twist. Webster 1828: extreme pain; anguish; the utmost degree of misery, either of body or mind. In the Authorized Version the word belongs to the demons’ dread, to the rich man in Luke 16, and to the final state of those who refuse the gospel.

Biblical Definition

The demons use the word first, and they use it of themselves. What have we to do with thee, Jesus, thou Son of God? art thou come hither to torment us before the time? (Matthew 8:29); the Gadarene cries I adjure thee by God, that thou torment me not (Mark 5:7). Two things follow: the demons know a time is appointed, and they know who will execute it. The clearest narrative use is our Lord’s own. The rich man in hell he lift up his eyes, being in torments, and seeth Abraham afar off (Luke 16:23), and pleads that his brothers be warned lest they also come into this place of torment (Luke 16:28). Revelation states the duration without softening: the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night (Revelation 14:11), and the devil, the beast, and the false prophet shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever (Revelation 20:10). Babylon’s fall is measured by it (Revelation 18:7, 10). The one gentle use points the other way: There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear: because fear hath torment (1 John 4:18) — the believer’s dread of judgment is what love drives out.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines TORMENT as extreme pain; anguish; the utmost degree of misery, either of body or mind; and, as a verb, to put to extreme pain or anguish. He notes the Scripture use of the future punishment of the wicked.

expand to see more

TORMENT, n. [L. tormentum, from torqueo, to twist.] — Extreme pain; anguish; the utmost degree of misery, either of body or mind.

That which gives pain, vexation or misery.

TORMENT, v.t. — To put to extreme pain or anguish; to inflict excruciating pain and misery, either of body or mind.

The Latin root is an instrument of torture, and the English kept the severity. The KJV does not use the word lightly, and neither should a preacher.

Key Scripture

Matthew 8:29 — "And, behold, they cried out, saying, What have we to do with thee, Jesus, thou Son of God? art thou come hither to torment us before the time?"

Luke 16:23 — "And in hell he lift up his eyes, being in torments, and seeth Abraham afar off, and Lazarus in his bosom."

Luke 16:28 — "For I have five brethren; that he may testify unto them, lest they also come into this place of torment."

Revelation 14:11 — "And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name."

1 John 4:18 — "There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear: because fear hath torment. He that feareth is not made perfect in love."

Modern Corruption

The doctrine these texts carry — eternal conscious punishment — is corrupted by annihilationism, which ends the torment in destruction, and by universalism, which ends it in restoration; both must set aside the plain duration Revelation states.

expand to see more

Annihilationism, or conditional immortality, holds that the lost are finally destroyed rather than punished without end, and it has gained ground among evangelicals in the last century. Revelation 14:11 is the text it must handle, and the handling is always the same: for ever and ever is read as the permanence of the outcome rather than the duration of the experience. But the verse adds they have no rest day nor night, which is a description of ongoing conscious experience, and Revelation 20:10 uses the identical phrase of the devil, whom no annihilationist supposes to be extinguished at the moment of sentence. The Lord Jesus, who spoke of hell more than anyone in Scripture, describes it as a place where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched (Mark 9:44).

Universalism runs the other way, holding that all are finally saved, and it must set aside Luke 16 in particular. The rich man is conscious, articulate, and in torment; Abraham tells him between us and you there is a great gulf fixed: so that they which would pass from hence to you cannot (Luke 16:26). The gulf is fixed, and it is fixed in a parable told by the Saviour Himself. The pastoral answer is not to soften the doctrine but to preach it as the demons apparently understand it — there is a time appointed and a Judge appointed — and then to preach 1 John 4:18, where the fear that has torment is cast out by a love that came to bear it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Greek noun basanos originally named a touchstone for testing metal, then the rack, then torment itself; the verb basanizo is what the demons dread and what Revelation predicts.

expand to see more

Greek basanos (G931) — a touchstone, then torture, then torment; being in torments (Luke 16:23) and fear hath torment (1 John 4:18).

Greek basanizo (G928) — to torment, to test by torture; art thou come hither to torment us before the time? (Matthew 8:29).

Greek basanismos (G929) — torment as an ongoing state; the smoke of their torment (Revelation 14:11), the fear of her torment (Revelation 18:10).

Greek eis aionas aionon — unto ages of ages, the phrase the KJV renders for ever and ever, used of God’s own eternity in the same book.

Greek kolasis (G2851) — punishment; everlasting punishment in Matthew 25:46, set in parallel with life eternal by the same adjective.

Usage

"Art thou come hither to torment us before the time? (Matthew 8:29) — the demons know a time is appointed and who will keep it."

"In hell he lift up his eyes, being in torments (Luke 16:23) — conscious experience after death, taught by Christ."

"Fear hath torment (1 John 4:18) — the dread of judgment, cast out by perfect love."
